blocks.x: Oh, that's pretty good. Yeah. I don't know why it's pretty good. It's much too loud. Okay. Ooh. That's the strangest thing. Okay. Let's talk and see if it records. Can you hear it?
Yeah, I hear it. Ooh. It's not supposed to make that noise.
I don't think there's anything in our steering wheel.
Ooh.
I couldn't do that before. Maybe if I hold it, maybe if I hold it, that'll be better. I can't understand why it's making that loud noise. You know.
Mm-hmm.

It didn't do that before when I was recording on it. I can't hear it. I can't hear it. I can't hear it. I can't hear it. I can't hear it. Well, let's just start talking and see if it records while we don't get any whine. So I want to say things like today's date is March 6th.
March 6th.
Yeah, 1972. And what's the address where we are?
1729, I think so. Yeah.
Yeah.
And your name is? Lawrence Turrell. Lawrence Turrell? Buddy Lawrence Turrell.
How do you spell your last name? T-U-R-A-U-G.
With a D on it?
Yeah. And where did you get the nickname of Buddy?
Well, most all the boys around this part of the town have got a little nickname.
Yeah. Did you get it when you were a child? Yeah, and I'd come up around O-T.
Yeah. Yeah. Where were you born? In Raffa? Were you born downtown?
Yeah, O-T, 22 years around. He kind of rolled. You were born there?
Mm-hmm. Really? What was that before there was a hall there? The hall was there. We lived there 20 years. Really? So you grew up there? How interesting.
Well, let me stop a minute and see if this is recording. That better stop. Okay. I hope I'm going to get aggravated. Okay. I hope I'm going to get aggravated. Okay. Okay.
The hall was there. Oh, no. The hall was there. We lived there 20 years.

Really? So you grew up there? Yeah. How interesting. Well, let me stop a minute and see if this is recording. That better stop. Okay. I can't understand what makes sense. Go up and down like that. It doesn't do it last night. Isn't that peculiar. I can't understand what makes us go up and down like that. It doesn't do it last night. Isn't that peculiar? Well. Well, let's go ahead and talk and see if your voice comes on a little stronger. I wanted to ask you, when did you leave, when did you move away from Economy Hall?
Well, I left Economy Hall when I went to the Army. Oh, I see. When I was twenty-two years old. I went to the camp.
Have you always lived downtown in this area? Yes, yes. All my life.
That's nice.
That's going nice. This is a beautiful part of the city. Did you go to dances and stuff at Economy Hall? Our dances was right there. Yeah. Right there.
Every weekend they danced Friday, Thursday, and Sunday. And sometimes Monday night.
Yeah. Well, did your family live upstairs?
Yeah, upstairs.
In the back of the hall?
Up in the back, yeah. My mother was a dentist.
Oh, I see. I see. Yeah. I see. They had a regular living place up there. Yeah, they were.
That's right.
That's right. That's right. Why did you decide to stay downtown? You never wanted to move anywhere else? Well, no.
I wasn't in there. I was young then. Yeah. When my mother was living, I had no other way to go but be with her and help her live.
Yeah. And did you have a big family? Lots of family?
I had six sisters. I mean seven sisters and three brothers.
Oh, that's a good size. Ten. Yeah, that's a good size family.
It's a great family. I got six living now and one Eve. Six sisters living and one Eve.
Oh, there's still most of them. Most of them lived in this neighborhood? They lived right back to St. Phil's.
Oh, yeah? 2210. That's good.
Everybody lived in the same neighborhood. Well, I want to ask you, did you ever hear a band leader named Two Roads?
No, there never was nobody ever was in a Two Roads when connected with men.
Yeah.
He most was contracted with Kaufman and different other kind of work.
I just wonder, cause I heard of a band leader named Two Roads. I wonder if it was in any relation to you? Yeah.

I never know them. I know that any musician would ever, ever put on a band stand. And practically, I supposedly made them all. Because I was the first one to put them before the public. Every musician was known. Oh, really?
That's right. Well, now tell me, did you run a home? Did you run a dance hall? Yeah.

I run, my mother was the genital one. I got big, we started giving dances every Sunday. And every Sunday I had a different band. At the Economy Hall. At the Economy Hall, yeah. And then after when I got older, I become the manager of the Gypsy Tea Room. And we brought all the big time bands in.
Yeah.

Lewis, Count Faison, Buddy Johnson, Cab Calloway, Sweetheart of the Rhythm, the Rhythm band. Now all the other ones, like, went up to Country and Made Good, Johnny Jots, Kid Ora's, George bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo I had a band going there. I lived in Oakland. Musicians down here. In the circuit. Punch. Chris Kelly. Keita Renee. Buddy Pettine.
They all stayed in New Orleans.
They all stayed in New Orleans. Yeah, I know. They all stayed in New Orleans. They got in the car before I came here. They all right from New Orleans, yeah.
Let me show it off a minute and see how this is recorded. I wanted to ask you, when did you start running the Gypsy Tea Room? Was it after you got out of the Army?
After I got out of the Army. And it was, it was a nightclub.
I never saw it.
It was a nightclub. It was a nightclub. It was run every night.
Was it one story or two stories?
One story.
Yeah. And it was, I know it was on Vilraside.
Vilraside.
Vilraside. Vilraside. On which corner?
Right on the, oh, Riverside. Riverside corner.
On the downtown?
No, Riverside. Yeah, the Riverside corner. Yeah, right on the corner. See, I never saw it they tore it down like before I came here.
Yeah, yeah.
See, it was.
How big was it? Did it have a big dance hall?
Yeah, 1,800 people.
Really? That big? That's fabulous. That's a fabulous big place.

Yeah, it was two, you see. We had a, when we had a small dance, we cut one part off. Yeah, I see. Like when we have a big band like Buddy Johnson and that. Yeah. We take that out and you got to, that's a whole block. Yeah. From Sinan to Orleans. Really? Mm-hmm.
Oh, that's great. Yeah. That's really great.
Yeah, 1,800 people. That's a lot of people.
How many bands did they have playing?
They had two bands. We had Sidney Deskene. He played from nine to ten, one hour.
Mm-hmm.
And the big band come on at ten and play from ten to two.
Who, well I thought Sidney Deskene had a big band. He did have a big band.
Yeah, he had a, like a swimming band. No, he had an 11th band. Yeah, that's a big band.
Yeah.
He had one of the best bands Y'all ever had. Yeah. A local band.
Who, were all his men from New Orleans?
All his men were right from New Orleans.
Who, do you remember who played in band this particular time?

Well, Joe Phillips, Professor Houston, himself, jazzed in the trumpet. Yes, he played the trumpet. Joe Phillips. Uh, Hold It Sam. Was a wonderful saxophone player. A big saxophone player. A bass saxophone player. A bass saxophone player? He took a little, big saxophone. They used to call it Hold It Sam. He used to hold that note, you know? Oh, I see.
Yeah, and uh…
Do you remember his last name?
No, I don't know.

Sam was his name, and they give him a name, Hold It Sam. Yeah, I see. But when he invented that record, hold it that, that number, they give him that name, Hold It Sam. But his name was Sam, but his last name, I didn't know it. Uh, we had another little band, Alvin Alcorn. Uh, yeah, a little seven piece band. They made up. It was a wonderful little band. But, I forgot all of them, but some of them died. Yeah.
Well, the most, did a lot of them leave town, or did most of them just stay here?
Yeah, all of them, that band moved and stood just. But the girls out of town come back, like Chester Jones, drum player, and uh, Willie Santiago, guitar player. Mm-hmm.
Well, it sounds like there are not that many musicians that left town for good. It sounds like most of the musicians just chose to live here, and…
Well, Alvin, one left the other day, went away and then he completely left here, and went away. When he first started, he started with my mother.
Mm-hmm.
At the Conner Hall.
Mm-hmm.

Uh, everybody was talking about Lewis Armstrong. He used to have a little band from the home, and every now and then they'd have a parade on Canal Street, and everybody would be talking about Lewis Armstrong. So, one day me and my mother was sitting in the kitchen, and I just had come from work. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I told my mother, I said, you know, sir, I got a good idea. I said, me and, uh, Captain Jones, the man, the head man at the home is good. I'm gonna see if I can get Cap to let Lewis come out of the home and play a little, uh, dance for you. Yeah. So, Professor, Professor Dave was his, uh, instructor. The old man would teach him how to play. Mm-hmm. And, uh, so I went and seen Cap, and, uh, he told me, sure, buddy. What you want? So, I went there and, uh, I spoke to him, so he said, yeah. So, I went out there, he said, what do you want? I said, well, I'm not got to deposit D that my mother gonna have the D ball. So, she selected D, and I went back there, he said, sure. When you get ready, let's come back here, and I'll make out of paper, and I'll release him under your kit. Mm-hmm. And I took him, and he had a hymn, drum, bass, and a guitar. Mm-hmm. And they didn't know, they didn't know but, but three pieces. Three pieces. They played that first piece, and then they jumped from that first piece to that third piece, and after they would play that, they'd come back to that first piece. Oh. And, uh, from three, I mean from three to six was for the children. Well, the children at that time was different than the children of today. And they didn't sell no strawberries, they didn't sell them but lemonade and oranges and apples. Well, that dance was from three to six for the children.
Mm-hmm.

And from six to four was for the growing ups. Yeah, I see. And that Sunday, at that hall, people going in and out, it was so crowded, eighteen hundred people passed through there. That's right. Wow. And, uh, we decided to, to make it like this. Uh, things was cheaper at that time. Uh, make a cheap, cheap admission, you see. Twenty-eight cents. Uh-huh. So we decided to get a ticket. Now, if you get one of these tickets, with this ticket, it is, uh, thirteen cents.
Uh-huh.

Without the ticket, it's twenty-eight cents. Uh-huh. You see, and that's where we draw the crowd. Everybody was running around looking for a ticket to save that thirteen cents. See, that was a good scheme. Oh, she did wonderful. Sounds like a good scheme. Yeah. What was your mother's name? Effie Two-Rolls. Effie?
Effie Two-Rolls.
That's pretty.
Real pretty.
Sounds like she was a good businesswoman. Mm-hmm.

You had her on the plane. Yeah. That was a beautiful building. I've, I've never seen a economy hall. They tore it down a couple of years before I came here, but I've seen pictures of it. It looks like a beautiful building. Oh, yeah.
A big building.
Oh, yeah. It's a beautiful building. I've, I've never seen a economy hall. They tore it down a couple of years before I came here, but I've seen pictures of it. It looks like a beautiful building.
Oh, it was fine.
It wasn't so big, but it was a real nice inside.

Yeah, that's where all the, the comical boards were given before they had the auditorium and all in places, you know, they built. And all the dances used to be there, the Illinois, the male carers, the Royal, Illinois, all in the Morrison cafeteria, and all of them used to get the big carnival dances there. Well, that's when I used to make a little chain. I used to do all the decorations in the hall and seat, and before that, and people all got burnt and gnatches in that fire. Yeah, I've read about that, the terrible fire and gnatches. That's what killed us. Yeah. A little job we used to get for $10, $15. Today, the decorated place like that cost you $300, $400. Really?
What kind of decorations would you use?
Well, that was crepe paper, with crepe.
Uh-huh. And you'd cover the ceiling?
Any way you wanted, we'd fix it. That's beautiful. Make it in blocks.
Then we'd twist it. That's beautiful.
Yeah.
Well, and then after the fire in Natchez, what did they have, did they have a, did they pass a law?
They passed a law, no more overhead, or crepe paper. How interesting. And before that, you would decorate the whole ceiling?
Would you decorate the walls too? We used to put wires across the ceiling, and we'd fix the paper over the wires, you know? Yeah, like you can wire. And you couldn't see the ceiling. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
After we put the paper there, it'd be so many different colors. It was beautiful. People used to come from all over, to come to see different places we used to fix. That's nice.
And was it, did you make it look like seams, like the scouts or something?

No, just blocks, but different colors. You see, we had hundreds of people come at the different ceiling, because that was a big ceiling, you see? Mm-hmm. And when Mr. Tessitore bought the place, the ceiling was in a bad condition, you see? So he sent for me, and he told me to come look at it, and I went look at it. He said, buddy, could you fix this up without me to have to put it in? I said, sure. I said, it's going to cost you a little money for paper. It's going to cost plenty of paper. He said, I don't care, I know it's going to cost me less than buying lumber and stuff. Great paper would be with 50 cents a box then. And he bought the paper thing and we fixed it. And Harold, because people used to come, Harold was playing at the Getsby Tee room there. His wife was working there with me then, she was in the floor show. Rose? Rose DeJong. Yeah, I know her. Yeah. We had eleven, I had 32 people working there counting the band under me. That's a bunch of people.
Well, what was it like at the Gypsy Tee room? They said they had a band and a floor show.
Floor show, two floor shows a night.
So it was just mostly dancing and the band would play for the dancing?
Yeah, yeah, singing, tap dancing. That's interesting. Yeah.
But did you have chairs and tables?
Oh yeah, we had tea with them, but tea.
Yeah.

And you'd sit down and drink and waiters. Seven wheels to wait on you. So it wasn't like a dance high, they didn't? Yeah, they had a speech piece dance, the table was around the side, under the balcony. See, we had a balcony. We had a balcony all around. Now if you want to go up in the balcony, you go up in the balcony. You want to sit downstairs? You sit down. Some people like to want to be private, they go upstairs in the balcony.
Yeah, I see.
I see.
But like the Gypsy Tea Room, was it ever connected with a social club or?
One man only. But so many social clubs give a fair as that.
They rent it, they would rent it?
No, you see the man would let them have the dues and he would have the concession, you see?
Who was the man who owned the place?
No, at that time when I decorated Johnny Tessitore.
Tessitore.
But when the Gypsy Tea Room was there, Louie Messina, who was the man that owned it.
Louie Messina?
Yeah, the promoter, the fight promoter.
And when was this?
Well, that was in, it's been, the Gypsy Tea Room been down now, but going on 10 or close to 12 years since they knocked it down. They condemned it. I didn't know I condemned it.
Yeah. So this was, what, after World War II? Yeah.
Right after World War I. Oh, right after World War I.
Yeah.
When you worked there.
Yeah. Well, what do you call that when you decorate ceiling? Is that like a trade? Does it have a name? Like, like being a plaster or a paper hanger or?

You have to cut it. Yeah. You have to cut it with a razor blade. You have to get a table, put it out there, make your measurements. To keep from getting out of line, you have to have them all the same size because it wouldn't look right. And when you put them up, they all in rotation. They hang just like this lamp, this lampshade. They hang just like that. I see. And it was all different colors. Beautiful scenery. Oh, yeah. That's really interesting.
I don't know they decorated the hall so fancy. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
It must have been beautiful. It took us, to fix that, it took us over a week and a half because that was a big ceiling. At the economy?
No, at the Gypsy Tears.

Oh, the Gypsy Tears. We had the wide points, crossing, and then we had to cut the paper to put up there. See, I had a father named Brother, Brother Fortuny, he's there now. Me and him used to work together, you see. And otherwise I couldn't do that by myself. Because I used to cut the paper and he'd hang it. He'd be up on the scapiscator coming down, I'd hand him the paper as he'd run out, you see. And go right along and we'd get through.
Where did you learn how to do that? Just pick it up.
Just pick it up.
It wasn't a trade you had to learn. No, no.
You could just pick it up.
That's really, really interesting.
Fascinating.

Well, who else played at the Gypsy Tears? When did Kid Rene play there? He played there at the time when I was a man. He was a house band. He was a house band. Yes. And that, did he? Harold was playing with him. Harold was? He was playing saxophone.
How interesting. Did he have a small band? Seven Peas. Uh huh.
And that, did he?
Harold was playing with him.
Harold was?
How interesting. Did he have a small band?
Seven Peas.
Uh huh. And that, did he?
How interesting. Did he have a small band? Seven Peas. Uh huh. Nice size.
That was a real good band.
No, that was after World War One.

He was one of the sweetest trumpet players you always have a poor them. With them. When he put them mute them there. Sweetest mute them the trumpet them. He was Lewis Lonezhong's right hand man. Lewis tried them them away over them. Oh really? A many times when his wife didn't want him to go.
So he, Kid Renai never left him alone.
No he died again. Yeah he died.
Him and his wife died. Well he was, was he older than Roy Armstrong?
No he was younger than Roy Armstrong.
Really?

Yeah, the name was about three, four years younger than, uh, Armstrong. But he was, when the Bulldog was in the home, he was about 12 years old, and Lewis was about 14 years old when he was back then.
Oh I see, so Lewis was a little bit older. I didn't realize that. That's funny.
Lewis was, when he was 70, some odd when he died, I believe in 72, right?
Something like that.
Yeah 72.
So Kid Renai wasn't very old.
He just wasted his life away. Yeah. What did he just drink too much?
He probably drank bad whiskey too.

He would still, when he knocked off his jaw, instead of going home, going and stay in the ballroom for him like to get off. At that time they played, they had to play from eight to four, and they'd get off and they'd go in the ballroom and stay in the 11th, sometimes 12 o'clock they'd be going home. Good lord. And they'd have nothing, they'd just drink it. Yeah. And they used to have some stuff they called Absinthe. They had all colors. Absinthe? Yeah, green, green, pink. What was that?
I've never had that.
That's a, that's a, that's a strong one of your own, that's not your heel. That's a strong one of your. Really strong? I wonder, hmm.
Yeah. Like green alcohol or moonshot or something?
Yeah, it's made out of alcohol. Yeah. But they colored it.
Oh, I see. So you'd drink it.

Yeah. With ice, you know, fresh ice. You ever know that? You ever know that? When they, when they, when they, when they, when they, when they, when they, at that price they used to drink that like they'd drink water. Really? 35 cents a half a pint. Yeah. You just sell gallons of that.
Yeah, that's pretty inexpensive.
Yeah, no, that wasn't no expensive. That was, well at that time, musicians used to play for a dollar a night.
Mm-hmm. And that was, they played for like eight hours or something?

Yeah, that seems funny. Yeah. A musician would play from, from nine o'clock at night to, they know when they're gonna play for one dollar. Mm-hmm. And today, they, they get from ten on up to play. Right. An hour.
Right.
Yeah. You see, that sure is different.
It sure is. That's cause I got a union now.

Now we used to, we used to take them, the band on a Sunday when we have our advertising with automobiles and decorate our cars and things. We all, we, with all different shirts and things and convertible cars and things. And we go, we have them from one, sometimes twelve o'clock in the day to five or six o'clock in the evening or on a Sunday. Mm-hmm. Then they had to play the ball that, that, that, uh, Monday night from eight to four. And it would be only $47. Wow. Now look at today. $47. Now you, I, I, like I'm gonna put this before the club for the, get, try to get this job for uh, to play only, uh, four hours, you tell me it's a hundred and ten dollars. Yeah, it is.
Yeah, for a six piece band I think. No, it's a four piece.
Four piece. Yeah.
Yeah, it's, it's, uh, the union is really out there now. Yeah. Man, they're tough. Ten dollars a pack.
They're tough on you.
What club are you working for now?
Uh, my club is The Last Man. The Last Man?
The Last Man Club.
Where, where's your club house?
Is it down, down around here?

We don't have no club. Oh, you don't now. We meet from house to house. Oh, I see. Each member has a, a meeting. Uh huh. We got twenty, twenty standing members. And every month, once a month, every month he'll have a meeting, and the next member he'll have a meeting.
Is it, is it a, a social club like the, like the, you know, the San Jacinto?
Oh no, that was a big club.
Yeah, well they, they had a regular club house.
Oh yeah, they had fifteen hundred members. Yeah, it's a social and pleasure club.
Yeah, that was, yeah, yeah.
Pool tables and everything. Yeah. Did you, did you ever work in the San Jacinto? I used to belong here. Oh yeah?
I was on the board of the Rickers.

How nice. That's a, that's a great old club. I've talked to a lot of the guys about that. Yeah, I was, I joined it and, uh, this boy, uh, Charlie Semarine, he was the chairman of the amusement committee. Uh huh. And, so, they wanted to examine the, and they put him on the board.
Uh huh.

And, so, the president told him, he would take and it was going to make him the, the chairman of the, of the board and he had to pick out nine members, besides himself, which would be the, to examine the books. And, uh, we, uh, got together and had a meeting and, and that was the worst night I ever seen. The first thing we went over was the, the, the treasure. Yeah. The treasure of the club had been went and, a finance company and drawed three hundred dollars on the Santa Center's name and then reported to the club. Good Lord.
That sounds like a humbug. Yeah.
And then we went down further, when we got through figuring the books out, the club was short of twenty two hundred dollars. Oh no.
I know. But when, when was this? Do you remember?
When the club was there, it was in about nineteen, it was in about nineteen, about nineteen, thirty five. Uh huh.
This was before Beansy took over.
Well Beansy, Beansy owned the building. Oh I see. He, he didn't own the building, uh, uh, when the, when the Santa Center had it. Uh huh. He bought the building after the Santa Center went broke.
Which was, which was after you did.
He bought the building, yeah.
Oh, well, well when, when you found out that the treasurer had, what had he done? He'd taken them, a. One. One. One. One. One. One. One. One. One.

There was a man named Monette. Monette, he was the secretary. Well, he used to collect money on the outside, and he'd go to the minor games, and take that money, and play minor, and with the time of the meeting come, he couldn't pay them people's money. What's a minor game, then? It was cards. You guessed the cards. You guessed them, you see? You guessed them, you pull them, you see? You put your money down on a card on the table, and if they pull that card, with your money on it, you win it. But if they don't pull it, you lose it. I'm not from here, I hadn't heard of that. I've heard a lot of games around here.

Now that looks like it's working fine. I think the little needles are moving. It's moving. Well, yeah, it's moving. It's moving. It has even up. I haven't done this very much. I get nervous about it. I wanted to ask you about the Green O. I know I've seen the Green O over there on North Claiborne Avenue in St. Philip. Oh, yeah. But it's not a bar now. It's a liquor store. It's just a liquor store. But it used to be a bar. No, never did. No? I thought it was at one time. No. Well, did you run it? Yes. But it was on the other corner. It was going up.
